The evidence clusters into two opposing camps: pro-use sources (d1, d2, d3, d5, d6) argue animals are necessary for safety/efficacy testing and legally required before human trials, while anti-use sources (d7, d8, d9, d10, d12) contend animal experiments are unreliable, cruel, and unnecessary given human-relevant alternatives. The retrieved evidence presents diametrically opposed positions on whether animals should be used for research, reflecting genuine conflicting opinions and research outcomes.

Proponents argue that animals are necessary because no substitute can replicate complex living systems, and U.S. federal law requires animal testing to demonstrate safety and efficacy before human trials [d1,d2,d5,d6]. They also emphasize animal welfare standards and the Three Rs framework in the EU, which aims to reduce and replace animal use over time [d3,d4]. In contrast, opponents argue that animal experiments are scientifically unreliable, often misleading, and cause unnecessary suffering; they advocate for human-relevant methods like cell-based microchips and high-fidelity simulators as better alternatives [d8,d10,d12]. Ethical arguments stress that animals have rights and should not be subjected to experimentation without consent [d7].

Given these conflicting viewpoints and research findings, there is no single agreed answer; the debate hinges on ethical values, scientific reliability, and regulatory frameworks.
